name: SmartGuard
description: Endpoint protection that produces compliance evidence. A Windows agent finds and stops threats on each company computer, including payment-card numbers left on laptops, and a console inside SmartComply's compliance platform lets the security team see and act on every computer at once, with every incident carried through to a ticket and an audit trail an auditor can read.
role: Senior software engineer: own the product end to end, agent, console and user guide
contributions: Own SmartGuard end to end: the Windows agent, its module in the compliance platform, and the user guide
Built PAN Scan: finds card numbers in files, SQLite databases and the saved-payment stores of Chrome, Edge and Firefox, shown masked, with quarantine or review in place

Built the live scan console: quick, full and custom scans with pause, resume and stop on the device and from the cloud; a live log with tabs, search, pinning and per-line actions; scan history; and export to reports, spreadsheets, SIEM and threat-intel formats
Built the Windows service that runs isolation, quarantine and scans sent from the console, with every action in the audit trail
Built the console's device-facing API (heartbeat, telemetry, command acknowledgements), playbook execution, indicators of compromise, tickets and scan control
Built the console pages: devices, device detail, threat review, live scan progress, tickets, playbooks, indicators and events
Defined one counting rule for threats so the app, the device page and the overview never disagree
Wrote the 140-page SmartGuard User Guide, and shipped the 19 display fixes writing it turned up
Reviewed and merged a colleague's real-time telemetry sync, API and web
results: 58 Rust modules, about 61,000 lines, 528 unit tests
210 console API routes and 22 playbook action types

body.heading: The problem
paragraphs: Small companies need endpoint protection, but auditors also ask how each incident was handled: who did what, and when. Most tools stop at "threat blocked", so the evidence ends up in screenshots and emails. SmartGuard carries every threat through to a ticket and an audit trail, linked to the compliance controls it is evidence for. It also finds payment-card numbers left on laptops, which PCI DSS cares about.

body.heading: My part
paragraphs: I joined SmartComply as a senior software engineer in July 2026 and own SmartGuard end to end: the Windows agent and desktop app, its whole module in the compliance platform (API, data model and pages), and the 140-page user guide. I become engineering manager in January.

body.heading: Finding card data
paragraphs: PAN Scan looks for card numbers in files, SQLite databases and the saved-payment stores of Chrome, Edge and Firefox. Each browser stores cards differently, and naive matching flags every long number, so a finding needs nearby payment context before it counts. The scan runs off the request thread with real progress and a configurable scope, shows only masked numbers, and lets each finding be quarantined or reviewed where it is.

body.heading: A scan you can watch
paragraphs: Quick, full and custom scans can be started, paused, resumed and stopped from the computer or from the cloud console, and both always agree on where a scan is, through restarts, dropped connections and late results. While it runs, the window shows files checked, threats found and how many are new, files it couldn't read, the speed and an honest estimate of the time left. Stopping asks first and says how many files are still unchecked; anything already found stays on the list.

body.heading: A log that explains itself
paragraphs: Every scan keeps a log, its diary: who started, paused, resumed or stopped it, which folders it checked, and every threat it found. Tabs sort the lines into threats, warnings, actions, progress and pinned lines; search highlights every match; and any line can be copied, pinned, narrowed to its folder, excluded from future scans or opened for the threat's details, with quarantine right there.

Scan history lists every scan on the computer, what it found, how many threats are still open and who started it, the user or the security team, and opens any of them back at its full log. A scan can be exported as a report for managers, findings for a spreadsheet, the raw log, full data, SIEM events or threat indicators for other security tools, with a choice to strip fingerprints and paths before sharing outside the company. Keyboard shortcuts cover the lot.

body.heading: Acting from the console
paragraphs: The security team can isolate a computer, quarantine a file or start a scan from the cloud console, and a separate Windows service carries it out without an admin prompt on the user's screen. Commands travel on the live stream and again in each heartbeat reply, so a command still reaches a device whose stream silently died; the agent de-duplicates them. Device-signed requests are rate-limited per device, not per address, and every action lands in the audit trail.

body.heading: Safe enough to trust
paragraphs: An agent that quarantines the wrong file is uninstalled by lunchtime. SmartGuard acts automatically only on exact identifications; anything merely suspicious raises an alert for a person to confirm. It never quarantines its own files or ordinary source code. Telemetry on the device is bounded by size, age and row count, so a cheap laptop's disk stays healthy, and the Events page says how far back it can see. A crash-loop sweep removed every crash it found.

body.heading: One set of numbers
paragraphs: The app, the device page and the console overview used to count threats differently. I defined what new, open and handled mean, and reconciled threats between the device and the cloud so every screen shows the same figures.

body.heading: A guide for people without a security team
paragraphs: SmartGuard is sold to companies without a security department, so I wrote the user guide for them: 140 pages with an annotated figure for every screen, plain explanations of why things work as they do, and personal data redacted from every screenshot. Writing it turned up 19 display problems, which I fixed.

body.heading: Built with
paragraphs: Rust with Tokio and Axum for the agent engine, SQLite on the device, YARA-X and Sigma rules for detection; Tauri, React, TypeScript, Zustand and Tailwind for the desktop app; an NSIS installer that bundles its runtime and frees locked files on reinstall. The console is Django REST Framework, PostgreSQL, Redis and Celery, with a React front end.
